issues.subcategory: false significance claim
issues.description: The discussion section explicitly states the meta-analytic effect size for Connection is 'significantly different from zero,' but the Results section reports p = .065 and a 95% CI of [-.01, .18] that includes zero. Both the p-value (>.05) and the CI (containing zero) indicate the result is NOT statistically significant at conventional thresholds. This is a direct factual error that misrepresents the primary outcome for this outcome variable.
issues.quote: However, the meta-analytic effect size was .09, and significantly different from zero.

issues.subcategory: FSN value contradiction across sections
issues.description: The Results section reports the Fail-Safe Number (FSN) for the Expression outcome as 3, while the Discussion section, in the same thematic paragraph about Expression, states 'only five unreported studies could reduce the results of the meta-analytic effect size p-value to nonsignificant.' FSN = 5 is reported for the Connection outcome in the Results. The wrong FSN value is imported into the Discussion for the wrong outcome, undermining the reliability of the authors' conclusions about Expression.
issues.quote: The FSN was 3 studies. [Results, Expression section] ... The FSN analysis, which indicated that only five unreported studies could reduce the results of the meta-analytic effect size p-value to nonsignificant, led us to be confident that future replications would find the same lack of an effect as our replications. [Discussion, Expression section]

issues.subcategory: prediction interval value discrepancy across sections
issues.description: The Results section reports the 95% Prediction Interval for Connection as [-.09, .26], while the Discussion section reports it as [-.07, .27]. These are numerically different intervals. The PI value actually matters substantively here because both versions include zero, but precise reporting is required for reproducibility and trust in the findings.
issues.quote: 95% PI [-.09, .26], p = .065. [Results] ... supported by the 95% PI of [-.07, .27], which includes zero. [Discussion]

issues.subcategory: original effect size inconsistently reported across sections and tables
issues.description: The original study's effect size for Self-Disclosure Advantages is reported as -.30 in the abstract and as '-.02 to -.30 vs. -.30' in the Results section, but as -.33 in Table 3 and as '-.02 to -.30 vs. -.33' in the Discussion. Table 1 shows the original β = -.300, while Table 3 lists original r = -0.33. Since the paper asserts β = r in simple regression, these should be identical. The discrepancy is unacknowledged and affects the interpretation of whether replications replicated the original effect.
issues.quote: self-esteem only weakly and inconsistently predicted perceived advantages of self-disclosure on Facebook (meta analytic effect size = -.16, original effect size = -.30) [Abstract] ... the effect sizes of all studies were descriptively less than or equal to the original (-.02 to -.30 vs. -.33) [Discussion]

issues.subcategory: studies included despite failing pre-specified minimum sample size
issues.description: The Methods section explicitly states the minimum sample size for the present replication was set at 120 ('120 for the present study to ensure adequate statistical power') and that 'all studies in this meta-analysis... collected the minimum number of participants specified by the CREP.' However, Table 1 shows that five of seven studies fall below N=120: BYU-Sp16 (N=90), BYU-Wi17 (N=90), Gordon (N=80), IIT-Sp17 (N=94), and SAU (N=81). This directly contradicts the methods claim and represents inclusion of underpowered studies in violation of the project's own pre-specified standards.
issues.quote: All studies in this meta-analysis received this approval by the CREP team, collected the minimum number of participants specified by the CREP (120 for the present study to ensure adequate statistical power)

issues.subcategory: conflation of confidence interval and prediction interval
issues.description: For the Expression outcome, the text states 'the 95% CI and prediction interval (PI) indicated future studies would show an effect size between .01 and .14' — presenting a single numerical range for both the CI and PI. The CI and PI are mathematically distinct and in practice PI is always wider than CI. Reporting a single interval for both is either an error (one was omitted) or a conflation that makes it impossible to distinguish precision of the meta-analytic estimate from expected variation in future studies.
issues.quote: the 95% CI and prediction interval (PI) indicated future studies would show an effect size between .01 and .14 (smaller than the original)

issues.subcategory: abstract misrepresents meta-analytic Expression result as null
issues.description: The abstract states 'self-esteem did not relate to perceived opportunities for self-expression (across the seven replications, all 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for effect sizes included zero).' However, the Results section reports the meta-analytic effect for Expression is r = .08, p = .021, 95% CI [.01, .14]—a statistically significant result with a CI that does not include zero. Referencing only individual-study CIs while ignoring the significant meta-analytic result in the abstract creates a materially misleading summary of the evidence.
issues.quote: self-esteem did not relate to perceived opportunities for self-expression (across the seven replications, all 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for effect sizes included zero) [Abstract] ... the point-estimate meta-analytic effect size of the seven replication studies, r = .08, p = .021 [Results]

issues.subcategory: composite scoring inconsistency unresolved
issues.description: The manuscript acknowledges that the Gordon study's composite score means implied items were summed rather than mean-averaged, which is inconsistent with the other studies. This difference would produce scores on different scales and is not trivially ignorable. However, the manuscript does not state whether the Gordon data were corrected prior to analysis or whether the scores as originally posted (potentially summed) were used. This gap makes it impossible for readers to evaluate the comparability of the Gordon data.
issues.quote: Two studies included analysis scripts that showed scores for all scales were mean averaged. The means for scores in most studies implied that the items were mean averaged, but the Gordon study's mean implied items were summed.

issues.subcategory: post-hoc meta-analytic model selection without pre-specified criterion
issues.description: The authors state they compared REML and DL estimation methods and selected REML because it 'produced more interpretable heterogeneity estimates for our data.' This selection was made after inspecting results, and the criterion ('more interpretable') is subjective and post-hoc. No pre-specification of which model would be used appears in the preregistration discussion. This represents an undisclosed researcher degree of freedom that could affect heterogeneity estimates, particularly problematic given the authors' own concerns about the reliability of heterogeneity statistics with small k.
issues.quote: We compared restricted maximum likelihood (REML) and DerSimonian and Laird (DL) models and selected REML as it produced more interpretable heterogeneity estimates for our data

issues.subcategory: inconsistent measurement scale format across studies
issues.description: Two studies (IIT-Sp16 and IIT-Sp17) used a 5-point response scale for the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale while the remaining five studies used the original 4-point scale. Changing the number of response options alters the psychometric properties of the scale and potentially the construct being measured. Both IIT studies come from the same lab and contribute two of seven data points; if the 5-point scale systematically affects scores, these studies introduce a confound that the meta-analysis does not model or adjust for.
issues.quote: most replications used the original four-point scale, while two replications (IIT-Sp16 and IIT-Sp17) used a five-point scale

issues.subcategory: group administration confound in one replication
issues.description: The SAU replication ran participants in groups of 2–6 rather than individually, while all other replications used individual or online administration. Group administration introduces social desirability effects, potential for participants to influence one another, and violations of the independence assumption for observations. The SAU sample produces the strongest Connection effect among replications (β = .237, p = .033) and is among the studies whose CI for Connection does not include zero. The possible confound between administration mode and results is not modeled.
issues.quote: Participants completing questionnaires in the lab did so alone, except for the SAU replication, which ran participants in groups of two to six.

issues.subcategory: derivation of original study's Expression effect size unexplained
issues.description: Table 1 records the original study's beta for Expression as 'n/a' because Forest and Wood (2012) did not report it. Yet Table 3 lists the original r for Express as 0.15, which is used for all difference-score comparisons in that table. The manuscript provides no explanation of how r = 0.15 was derived from the original study given that the β was unavailable. Without this explanation, readers cannot verify whether this value is accurate.
issues.quote: * The original study did not report a beta coefficient for this variable. [Table 1 note] ... BYU-Sp16 | 0.18 | 0.15 [Table 3, Express original r]

issues.subcategory: no standardized missing data protocol across studies
issues.description: The manuscript acknowledges that not all contributing teams documented their missing data handling procedures, exclusion criteria, or composite scoring decisions. Because these decisions can meaningfully alter sample sizes and effect sizes, the absence of standardized and documented protocols means that ostensibly identical analyses may differ in undisclosed ways. The meta-analysis therefore aggregates results that may differ not just due to true sampling variability but due to differential data handling.
issues.quote: not all studies posted analysis scripts or narratives to help us determine such things as missing data handling, composite score calculations, data exclusions, etc. Data were not always collected or stored consistently

issues.subcategory: causal language applied to cross-sectional correlational data
issues.description: Throughout the paper, self-esteem is described as 'predicting' Facebook perceptions and as causing individuals with low self-esteem to 'prefer' or 'use' Facebook for compensation. Social compensation theory is invoked as a causal mechanism. However, all data are cross-sectional and correlational; self-esteem and Facebook perceptions are measured at the same time point. Reverse causation (Facebook experiences affecting self-esteem) and third-variable confounds (e.g., social anxiety, personality traits) are not addressed.
issues.quote: Our meta-analysis confirmed the original study's findings that when compared with individuals high in self-esteem, those with low self-esteem saw Facebook as a safer and more advantageous way of self-disclosing relative to FTF interactions. The present research also provides some support for social compensation theory... This theory suggests that for those with lower self-esteem, the anxiety provoked by FTF interactions can be somewhat mitigated in online interactions.

issues.subcategory: systematic opposite-direction effect for Expression ignored
issues.description: Social compensation theory predicts that those with lower self-esteem will perceive Facebook as better for self-expression, implying a negative relationship between self-esteem and expression perceptions. However, the original study (r = +0.15) and six of seven replications show a positive relationship—the opposite direction. The only discussion of this pattern is to note the non-significance of the effects; the consistent directional reversal relative to theoretical prediction is never acknowledged or theoretically explained.
issues.quote: Consistent with the original study, all seven replications showed that self-esteem was not a significant predictor of participants seeing Facebook as enabling them to express themselves.

issues.subcategory: publication bias argument misapplied to non-significant original finding
issues.description: The authors claim that the smaller meta-analytic effect for Expression compared to the original's r = 0.15 is 'consistent with original study's larger susceptibility to publication bias.' However, the original Expression finding was non-significant (p = .181). Publication bias operates by suppressing null results and inflating significant ones; it does not apply to findings the original authors themselves reported as null. Invoking publication bias to explain a non-significant result is a category error.
issues.quote: all factors indicating the presence of publication bias in the original study

issues.subcategory: exclusively undergraduate WEIRD sample with no caveat
issues.description: All seven replications and the original study draw exclusively from undergraduate student populations at U.S. institutions. Facebook's two billion users are predominantly non-students and span a wide age range globally. The manuscript notes cultural differences briefly in the context of a Turkish study, but does not systematically acknowledge that findings from U.S. undergraduates may not generalize to older adults, non-students, non-Western populations, or even U.S. adults with different Facebook usage motivations.
issues.quote: Participants in all studies were undergraduate students at the five universities and colleges in the US where the replications were conducted

issues.subcategory: platform relevance shift undermines Facebook measure validity
issues.description: The Facebook perceptions measure was created in 2012 for a context where Facebook was the primary social network for young adults. The replications were conducted in 2016–2017, by which time Instagram and Snapchat had substantially displaced Facebook for self-expression and social interaction among college-aged users. The discussion acknowledges this shift but does not treat it as a threat to construct validity: if participants are mentally comparing Facebook to Instagram/Snapchat when completing the measure, the construct being assessed may differ systematically from what was assessed in the original study.
issues.quote: Participants in our replication studies may have been implicitly comparing Facebook usage to Snapchat and Instagram when rating its usefulness for self-expression and connection with others, whereas these platforms would not have been a consideration for participants in Forest and Wood's (2012) study.

issues.subcategory: Table 2 content absent from manuscript
issues.description: The Results section states 'Table 2 shows each study's descriptive statistics for gender, race, and the mean and standard deviation for self-esteem and each of the four outcome variables,' and the text references Table 2 for demographic statistics. In the provided manuscript, Table 2 contains only the note 'n/a = Data not available. n/c = Data not collected' with no actual data. Without these descriptive statistics, readers cannot assess baseline comparability across samples or identify potential confounds.
issues.quote: Table 2 shows each study's descriptive statistics for gender, race, and the mean and standard deviation for self-esteem and each of the four outcome variables.

issues.subcategory: original study regression model specification not confirmed
issues.description: The paper treats standardized β as equivalent to r throughout, which is valid only in simple regression with a single predictor. The manuscript never confirms that the original Forest and Wood (2012) Study 1 used simple (rather than multiple) regression. If the original study included covariates (e.g., age, gender, Facebook use frequency), β ≠ r, and the effect sizes extracted for Table 3 would be incorrect. The original study's regression specification should be explicitly stated and the equivalence assumption justified.
issues.quote: Beta coefficients are standardized (consistent with the original research). Effect size r is equivalent to the beta coefficient.

issues.subcategory: sign convention for effect size difference undefined in Table 3
issues.description: Table 3 presents 'Difference' values for each replication-vs-original comparison but does not define the direction of subtraction (replication minus original, or original minus replication). Inspection of the data suggests the formula is original minus replication, but this is never stated. For Safety in BYU-Sp16, the replication r = +0.08 and the original r = -.31 yield a difference listed as -.39, consistent with original minus replication. The unsigned column header makes it impossible to independently verify the differences without inference, and the text's interpretation of significance depends on this sign convention.
issues.quote: Study | Replication r | Original r | Difference | 95% CI

issues.subcategory: item wording differences in IIT-Sp16 not evaluated for measurement equivalence
issues.description: The IIT-Sp16 replication used four RSE items with altered wording (e.g., 'I think I am no good at all' vs. 'At times I think I am no good at all'). Item wording changes can alter item difficulty, factor loadings, and scale reliability, yet no measurement equivalence or differential item functioning analysis is reported. IIT-Sp16 also uses the 5-point scale variant. Together these modifications make IIT-Sp16 the most methodologically deviant study, yet it is included without adjustment or sensitivity analysis.
issues.quote: one study (IIT-Sp16) had slight differences in item order and in wording on four out of ten items (e.g., 'At times I think I am no good at all' vs. 'I think I am no good at all')

issues.subcategory: preregistration scope limited to individual study level with no overarching meta-analytic preregistration
issues.description: The paper claims preregistration badges for each individual study's data collection and analysis plans, but acknowledges that the meta-analytic synthesis itself was not preregistered at a central level. Decisions made in the meta-analysis—which studies to include, which model to use (REML vs. DL), how to handle the Gordon scoring discrepancy, and the choice to exclude heterogeneity moderator analyses—were made post-hoc without a prospective analysis plan. The meta-level analytic decisions are thus not covered by any preregistration.
issues.quote: the data collection and data analysis methods were preregistered at each individual study's OSF page
